notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Electronics is the branch of science and engineering dealing with controlled flow of electrons or other charge carriers in devices and circuits.
  • Modern electronics is largely based on semiconductor materials.
  • Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor.
  • Germanium is another important semiconductor.
  • Electronic devices are used for amplification, switching, computation, sensing, communication and control.
  • Semiconductor devices are generally smaller, faster and more energy-efficient than older vacuum-tube devices.
  • Modern computers, smartphones, televisions and control systems depend on integrated electronic circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electronics → Semiconductor Devices + Control of Electric Signals

2. Conductors
  • Conductors allow electric current to flow easily.
  • Metals are generally good conductors.
  • Copper is widely used in electrical wiring.
  • Conductors contain large numbers of mobile charge carriers.
  • Their electrical resistance is relatively low.
3. Insulators
  • Insulators strongly resist electric-current flow.
  • Rubber, glass, plastic and ceramic are common insulators.
  • Insulators have very few free charge carriers under ordinary conditions.
  • Their resistivity is very high.
4. Semiconductors
  • Semiconductors have electrical conductivity between conductors and insulators.
  • Silicon and germanium are elemental semiconductors.
  • Semiconductor conductivity can be controlled by temperature, light, electric fields and doping.
  • Semiconductors form the basis of diodes, transistors and integrated circuits.
  • Semiconductor resistance generally decreases as temperature increases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Silicon + Germanium → Semiconductors

5. Silicon
  • Silicon has atomic number 14.
  • Silicon has four valence electrons.
  • It is a Group 14 element.
  • Silicon forms covalent bonds in its crystal lattice.
  • Silicon is the dominant semiconductor used in integrated circuits.
  • Silicon is abundant in Earth's crust mainly in compounds such as silica and silicates.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Silicon → 4 Valence Electrons → Main IC Semiconductor

6. Germanium
  • Germanium has atomic number 32.
  • It has four valence electrons.
  • Germanium was important in early semiconductor devices.
  • Germanium has a smaller band gap than silicon.
  • Germanium devices generally have greater leakage current than comparable silicon devices.
7. Energy Bands

Important energy regions in solids include:

  • Valence band.
  • Conduction band.
  • Forbidden energy gap.
  • The arrangement of these bands determines electrical behaviour.
8. Valence Band
  • Valence band contains electrons involved in bonding.
  • In semiconductors, electrons can be excited from valence band to conduction band.
  • Vacancies left behind in the valence band behave as holes.
9. Conduction Band
  • Electrons in the conduction band can move through the material and carry current.
  • Conductors have readily available mobile electrons.
  • In semiconductors, energy must usually be supplied to create sufficient conduction-band electrons.
10. Band Gap
  • Band gap is the energy difference between valence and conduction bands.
  • Conductors have overlapping bands or essentially no forbidden gap in simplified models.
  • Semiconductors have a small band gap.
  • Insulators have a relatively large band gap.
  • Band-gap energy affects optical and electrical properties.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Small Band Gap → Semiconductor

Large Band Gap → Insulator

11. Intrinsic Semiconductor
  • An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor.
  • Pure silicon is an intrinsic semiconductor.
  • Pure germanium is an intrinsic semiconductor.
  • Thermal energy creates electron-hole pairs.
  • Number of electrons equals number of holes in an ideal intrinsic semiconductor.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Intrinsic → Pure Semiconductor

12. Electron-Hole Pair
  • When a valence electron gains sufficient energy, it can enter the conduction band.
  • The missing electron leaves a vacancy called a hole.
  • The electron and hole form an electron-hole pair.
  • Both electrons and holes contribute to current in semiconductors.
13. Hole
  • A hole is an absence of an electron in a valence-band state.
  • It behaves as an effective positive charge carrier.
  • Holes are not separate fundamental particles.
  • Hole motion corresponds to successive movement of valence electrons.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hole → Effective positive carrier, not a proton.

14. Doping
  • Doping is deliberate addition of controlled impurities to a pure semiconductor.
  • Doping increases and controls conductivity.
  • Doped semiconductor is called an extrinsic semiconductor.
  • Doping produces n-type or p-type semiconductor.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Doping → Extrinsic Semiconductor

15. Extrinsic Semiconductor

Two major types are:

  • n-type semiconductor.
  • p-type semiconductor.
  • Majority-carrier type depends on dopant.
16. n-Type Semiconductor
  • n-type semiconductor is produced by adding pentavalent impurity to silicon or germanium.
  • Pentavalent dopants have five valence electrons.
  • One electron is loosely available for conduction.
  • Electrons are majority carriers.
  • Holes are minority carriers.
  • n-type material remains electrically neutral overall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

n-Type → Pentavalent → Electrons Majority

17. Pentavalent Dopants

Common donor impurities include:

  • Phosphorus.
  • Arsenic.
  • Antimony.
  • They have five valence electrons.
  • They donate extra electrons.
  • They are called donor impurities.
📌 Remember

n-Type → Donor → P, As, Sb

18. p-Type Semiconductor
  • p-type semiconductor is produced by adding trivalent impurity.
  • Trivalent dopants have three valence electrons.
  • They create holes in the crystal lattice.
  • Holes are majority carriers.
  • Electrons are minority carriers.
  • p-type semiconductor remains electrically neutral overall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

p-Type → Trivalent → Holes Majority

19. Trivalent Dopants

Common acceptor impurities include:

  • Boron.
  • Aluminium.
  • Gallium.
  • Indium.
  • They create holes.
  • They are called acceptor impurities.
📌 Remember

p-Type → Acceptor → B, Al, Ga, In

20. Majority and Minority Carriers
  • n-type majority carriers → Electrons.
  • n-type minority carriers → Holes.
  • p-type majority carriers → Holes.
  • p-type minority carriers → Electrons.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

n-type is not negatively charged overall.

p-type is not positively charged overall.

Both remain electrically neutral.

21. p–n Junction
  • A p–n junction is formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductor regions.
  • Electrons diffuse from n-side toward p-side.
  • Holes diffuse from p-side toward n-side.
  • Recombination occurs near the junction.
  • A depletion region forms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

p + n → Junction → Depletion Region

22. Depletion Region
  • Depletion region contains very few mobile charge carriers.
  • It contains fixed ionised donor and acceptor atoms.
  • An internal electric field develops.
  • This produces a potential barrier.
  • The barrier opposes further majority-carrier diffusion.
23. Barrier Potential
  • Barrier potential develops across a p–n junction.
  • It depends on semiconductor material and temperature.
  • Typical room-temperature values often used in basic electronics are about 0.7 V for silicon and about 0.3 V for germanium.
  • These are approximate practical values, not universal constants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Silicon Junction → ~0.7 V

Germanium Junction → ~0.3 V

24. Semiconductor Diode
  • A diode is a two-terminal semiconductor device.
  • It contains one p–n junction in the basic form.
  • Its terminals are called anode and cathode.
  • A diode allows current readily in one direction and strongly restricts it in the opposite direction.
  • Diodes are used for rectification, protection and signal processing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diode → One-Way Current Device

25. Forward Bias
  • A p–n junction is forward biased when p-side is connected toward positive potential and n-side toward negative potential.
  • Forward bias reduces barrier potential.
  • Depletion region narrows.
  • Significant current can flow after sufficient forward voltage is applied.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Forward Bias → P to Positive, N to Negative

26. Reverse Bias
  • A p–n junction is reverse biased when p-side is connected toward negative potential and n-side toward positive potential.
  • Reverse bias increases barrier potential.
  • Depletion region widens.
  • Only a very small reverse current flows in an ordinary diode until breakdown.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reverse Bias → P to Negative, N to Positive

27. Diode Characteristic
  • Forward current rises rapidly after the junction reaches its effective turn-on region.
  • Reverse current is very small under ordinary reverse bias.
  • At sufficiently high reverse voltage, breakdown can occur.
  • Breakdown may damage an ordinary diode unless it is designed for that mode.
28. Rectification
  • Rectification is conversion of alternating current into unidirectional current.
  • Semiconductor diodes are widely used as rectifiers.
  • Rectifiers are used in power supplies.
  • Rectifier output usually requires filtering to obtain smoother DC.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rectifier → AC to DC

29. Half-Wave Rectifier
  • A half-wave rectifier uses one diode in its simplest form.
  • It allows one half-cycle of AC to reach the load.
  • The other half-cycle is blocked.
  • The output is pulsating DC.
  • It has relatively large ripple.
30. Full-Wave Rectifier
  • A full-wave rectifier uses both halves of the AC waveform.
  • It produces pulsating DC with higher average output than a half-wave rectifier.
  • It has lower ripple frequency spacing and is easier to filter.
  • It may use a centre-tapped transformer with two diodes or a bridge arrangement.
31. Bridge Rectifier
  • A bridge rectifier commonly uses four diodes.
  • It provides full-wave rectification.
  • It does not require a centre-tapped transformer.
  • Current through the load remains in the same direction during both AC half-cycles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bridge Rectifier → 4 Diodes

32. Filter Circuit
  • A filter smooths the pulsating output of a rectifier.
  • Capacitors are commonly used as filters.
  • Capacitor charges near voltage peaks.
  • It discharges between peaks.
  • This reduces ripple in the output voltage.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rectifier + Filter → Smoother DC

33. Ripple
  • Ripple is unwanted AC variation remaining in rectified DC output.
  • Full-wave rectification generally gives less ripple than half-wave rectification for similar filtering conditions.
  • Filter circuits reduce ripple.
34. Zener Diode
  • A Zener diode is designed to operate safely in reverse breakdown.
  • It can maintain an approximately constant voltage over a useful current range.
  • Zener diodes are widely used for voltage regulation and reference voltage.
  • They are normally reverse biased during regulation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zener Diode → Voltage Regulation → Reverse Bias

35. Light-Emitting Diode
  • LED stands for Light-Emitting Diode.
  • LED emits light when forward biased.
  • Electron-hole recombination releases energy as photons.
  • LEDs are highly energy-efficient.
  • They have long operating life.
  • They are used in displays, indicators and lighting.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LED → Forward Bias → Emits Light

36. LED Colours
  • LED colour depends mainly on semiconductor band gap.
  • Different semiconductor materials produce different wavelengths.
  • Red LEDs generally have lower photon energy than blue LEDs.
  • Blue photons have higher energy than red photons.
37. White LED
  • White LEDs commonly use a blue or ultraviolet LED with phosphor materials.
  • Phosphor converts part of the emitted light to other wavelengths.
  • Combined wavelengths appear white to the human eye.
38. LED vs Incandescent Lamp
  • LEDs convert a larger fraction of electrical energy into visible light.
  • Incandescent lamps produce much more heat.
  • LEDs have longer life.
  • LEDs require semiconductor electronic control in many lighting products.
39. Photodiode
  • A photodiode converts incident light into electrical current or voltage.
  • It is commonly operated in reverse bias.
  • Light creates electron-hole pairs.
  • Photodiodes are used in optical communication, sensors and light detectors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Photodiode → Light Detector → Reverse Bias Commonly

40. Solar Cell
  • A solar cell converts light directly into electrical energy.
  • It operates through the photovoltaic effect.
  • It is a semiconductor p–n junction device.
  • Silicon is widely used.
  • Solar cells produce DC electricity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solar Cell → Photovoltaic Effect → Light to DC

41. Photovoltaic Effect
  • Photovoltaic effect is generation of voltage and current when light is absorbed in suitable materials.
  • Electron-hole pairs are created.
  • Built-in electric fields separate charge carriers.
  • Solar cells use this effect.
42. LDR
  • LDR stands for Light Dependent Resistor.
  • Its resistance changes with light intensity.
  • In a typical LDR, resistance decreases as light intensity increases.
  • LDRs are used in automatic streetlights and light sensors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LDR → Light ↑, Resistance ↓

43. Thermistor
  • A thermistor is a temperature-sensitive resistor.
  • NTC thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises.
  • PTC thermistor resistance increases as temperature rises.
  • Thermistors are used in temperature sensing and protection circuits.
44. Transistor
  • A transistor is a semiconductor device used for amplification and switching.
  • It revolutionised electronic technology by replacing many vacuum-tube applications.
  • Bipolar junction transistor has three semiconductor regions.
  • Common BJT types are NPN and PNP.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Transistor → Amplifier + Switch

45. Invention of Transistor
  • The first successful point-contact transistor was demonstrated in 1947.
  • John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built it at Bell Laboratories.
  • William Shockley developed important transistor theory and junction-transistor concepts.
  • Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Transistor → 1947 → Bardeen + Brattain + Shockley

46. Bipolar Junction Transistor
  • BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor.
  • It contains two p–n junctions.
  • It has three terminals.
  • Terminals are emitter, base and collector.
  • Two basic types are NPN and PNP.
47. Emitter
  • The emitter is heavily doped.
  • It supplies majority carriers.
  • In an NPN transistor, electrons are supplied from emitter.
  • In a PNP transistor, holes are supplied from emitter.
48. Base
  • Base is very thin.
  • It is lightly doped compared with emitter.
  • A small base current can control a much larger collector current in a BJT.
  • The thin base allows most injected carriers to reach the collector.
49. Collector
  • Collector collects charge carriers coming through the base region.
  • It is physically designed to handle greater power than the base.
  • Collector current forms the main controlled current in amplification applications.
50. NPN Transistor
  • NPN transistor consists of n-p-n semiconductor regions.
  • Electrons are the main carriers injected by emitter.
  • A small base current controls a larger collector current.
  • NPN transistors are widely used in electronic circuits.
51. PNP Transistor
  • PNP transistor consists of p-n-p regions.
  • Holes are the main carriers injected by emitter.
  • Conventional current directions are opposite to corresponding NPN current directions.
52. Transistor Current Relation

For a BJT:

  • Emitter current = Collector current + Base current.
  • IE = IC + IB.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

IE = IC + IB

53. Current Gain
  • Common-emitter current gain is represented by β.
  • β = IC/IB.
  • A small base current can therefore control a larger collector current.
  • β varies with transistor and operating conditions.
54. Transistor as Amplifier
  • An amplifier increases the amplitude or power of an electrical signal.
  • A small input variation can control a larger output variation.
  • Transistors are used in audio, radio and sensor amplifiers.
  • Amplification requires an external energy source.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

An amplifier does not create energy; it controls energy supplied by the power source.

55. Transistor as Switch
  • A transistor can operate in OFF and ON states.
  • In digital electronics, these states can represent binary 0 and 1.
  • Transistor switches are used in computers and control circuits.
  • Billions of transistor switches can be integrated on modern chips.
56. Field-Effect Transistor
  • FET stands for Field-Effect Transistor.
  • It is primarily a voltage-controlled device.
  • Current through a channel is controlled by an electric field.
  • FETs have very high input impedance.
  • Major types include JFET and MOSFET.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

FET → Voltage-Controlled Device

57. MOSFET
  • MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor.
  • MOSFET is the dominant transistor technology in digital integrated circuits.
  • It has gate, source and drain terminals.
  • Gate voltage controls channel conduction.
  • MOSFETs have extremely important roles in processors and memory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Modern Digital IC → MOSFET

58. BJT vs FET
  • BJT is often described as a current-controlled device.
  • FET is primarily voltage controlled.
  • BJT involves both electrons and holes in operation.
  • FET conduction is mainly controlled through one carrier type in a channel.
  • FET generally has higher input impedance.
59. SCR
  • SCR stands for Silicon Controlled Rectifier.
  • It is a four-layer semiconductor switching device.
  • It belongs to the thyristor family.
  • It has anode, cathode and gate terminals.
  • A gate pulse can trigger conduction.
  • SCRs are used in power-control circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SCR → Controlled High-Power Switching

60. Diode vs Transistor
  • Basic diode → Two terminals.
  • BJT transistor → Three terminals.
  • Diode primarily allows one-way conduction.
  • Transistor is used mainly for switching and amplification.
61. Analog Electronics
  • Analog signals vary continuously with time or amplitude.
  • Microphone output is naturally analog before digitisation.
  • Temperature sensor voltage may be analog.
  • Analog circuits process continuous signals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Analog → Continuous

62. Digital Electronics
  • Digital electronics uses discrete signal levels.
  • Binary digital systems commonly use two states.
  • These states are represented as 0 and 1.
  • Modern computers operate primarily using digital logic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Digital → Discrete → 0 and 1

63. Binary Number System
  • Binary uses base 2.
  • Digits are 0 and 1.
  • Each binary digit is called a bit.
  • Position values are powers of 2.
  • Electronic logic circuits naturally represent binary states.
64. Bit
  • Bit stands for binary digit.
  • One bit can represent 0 or 1.
  • Bit is the smallest basic unit of digital information.
65. Nibble
  • A nibble consists of 4 bits.
  • Two nibbles make one byte.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 Nibble = 4 Bits

66. Byte
  • One byte conventionally consists of 8 bits.
  • Bytes are widely used for computer data representation.
  • 1 byte = 8 bits.
📌 Must-Memorise

1 Byte = 8 Bits

67. Decimal to Binary — Basic Facts
  • Decimal 0 → Binary 0.
  • Decimal 1 → Binary 1.
  • Decimal 2 → Binary 10.
  • Decimal 3 → Binary 11.
  • Decimal 4 → Binary 100.
  • Decimal 8 → Binary 1000.
68. Logic Gates
  • Logic gates are basic building blocks of digital circuits.
  • They perform Boolean operations.
  • Common gates are AND, OR and NOT.
  • Other gates include NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR.
69. AND Gate
  • AND gate gives output 1 only when all required inputs are 1.
  • For two inputs:
  • 0 AND 0 → 0.
  • 0 AND 1 → 0.
  • 1 AND 0 → 0.
  • 1 AND 1 → 1.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

AND → All 1 gives 1

70. OR Gate
  • OR gate gives output 1 when at least one input is 1.
  • For two inputs:
  • 0 OR 0 → 0.
  • 0 OR 1 → 1.
  • 1 OR 0 → 1.
  • 1 OR 1 → 1.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

OR → Any 1 gives 1

71. NOT Gate
  • NOT gate has one input.
  • It produces the opposite logical state.
  • Input 0 → Output 1.
  • Input 1 → Output 0.
  • NOT gate is also called inverter.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NOT → Inverter

72. NAND Gate
  • NAND means NOT-AND.
  • It gives output 0 only when all inputs are 1.
  • In all other two-input combinations, output is 1.
  • NAND is a universal gate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NAND → Universal Gate

73. NOR Gate
  • NOR means NOT-OR.
  • It gives output 1 only when all inputs are 0.
  • Otherwise output is 0.
  • NOR is a universal gate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NOR → Universal Gate

74. Universal Gates
  • NAND is a universal gate.
  • NOR is a universal gate.
  • Any other basic logic function can be constructed using only NAND gates.
  • Any basic logic function can also be constructed using only NOR gates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Universal Gates → NAND + NOR

75. XOR Gate
  • XOR stands for Exclusive OR.
  • For two inputs, output is 1 when inputs are different.
  • 0 XOR 0 → 0.
  • 0 XOR 1 → 1.
  • 1 XOR 0 → 1.
  • 1 XOR 1 → 0.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

XOR → Different Inputs → 1

76. XNOR Gate
  • XNOR is the complement of XOR.
  • It gives output 1 when two inputs are the same.
  • 0 XNOR 0 → 1.
  • 1 XNOR 1 → 1.
  • Different inputs give 0.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

XNOR → Same Inputs → 1

77. Boolean Algebra
  • Boolean algebra deals with logical variables having values 0 and 1.
  • It was developed by George Boole.
  • It forms the mathematical foundation of digital logic.
  • AND corresponds to logical multiplication.
  • OR corresponds to logical addition.
  • NOT corresponds to complementation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

George Boole → Boolean Algebra

78. Important Boolean Identities
  • A + 0 = A.
  • A + 1 = 1.
  • A·0 = 0.
  • A·1 = A.
  • A + A = A.
  • A·A = A.
  • A + A̅ = 1.
  • A·A̅ = 0.
79. De Morgan's Laws
  • NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B.
  • NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.
  • De Morgan's laws are fundamental in logic-circuit simplification.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Complement of AND → OR of Complements

Complement of OR → AND of Complements

80. Combinational Circuit
  • Output of a combinational circuit depends only on present inputs.
  • It has no memory of previous states.
  • Adders and multiplexers are examples.
  • Logic gates can be combined to form combinational circuits.
81. Sequential Circuit
  • Sequential-circuit output depends on present inputs and previous state.
  • It therefore contains memory.
  • Flip-flops are basic memory elements.
  • Counters and registers are sequential circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sequential Circuit → Has Memory

82. Flip-Flop
  • A flip-flop is a bistable digital circuit.
  • It can store one bit of information.
  • Common types include SR, JK, D and T flip-flops.
  • Flip-flops are used in registers, counters and memory circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 Flip-Flop → 1 Bit

83. Register
  • A register stores a group of bits.
  • Registers are made from flip-flops.
  • They are used for temporary data storage inside digital systems.
  • Processor registers operate at very high speed.
84. Counter
  • A digital counter follows a sequence of binary states.
  • Counters are used in clocks, timers and frequency measurement.
  • They are usually constructed from flip-flops and logic gates.
85. Clock Signal
  • Digital sequential circuits often use a clock signal.
  • A clock provides regular timing pulses.
  • Clock frequency is measured in hertz.
  • Processor speed is often specified in MHz or GHz.
86. Oscillator
  • An oscillator generates a periodic electrical signal without a periodic external input.
  • Electronic oscillators may produce sine, square or other waveforms.
  • Oscillators are used in clocks, transmitters and processors.
  • Feedback is commonly used.
87. Quartz Crystal Oscillator
  • Quartz crystals exhibit the piezoelectric effect.
  • They vibrate at stable resonant frequencies.
  • Quartz oscillators provide accurate timing.
  • They are used in watches, computers and communication equipment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Quartz → Stable Electronic Timing

88. Piezoelectric Effect
  • Certain crystals produce electric voltage when mechanically stressed.
  • This is the direct piezoelectric effect.
  • Applying voltage can also produce mechanical deformation.
  • Quartz is a piezoelectric material.
  • Piezoelectric devices are used in sensors and ultrasound transducers.
89. Integrated Circuit
  • IC stands for Integrated Circuit.
  • An IC contains many electronic components fabricated on a small semiconductor chip.
  • Components can include transistors, diodes, resistors and capacitors.
  • Silicon is the most common IC substrate.
  • ICs greatly reduce size and cost of electronic systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

IC → Many Components on One Chip

90. Invention of Integrated Circuit
  • Jack Kilby demonstrated an early working integrated circuit in 1958.
  • Robert Noyce independently developed a practical monolithic integrated circuit concept using planar silicon technology around 1959.
  • Kilby received part of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for work leading to integrated circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jack Kilby + Robert Noyce → Integrated Circuit

91. IC Integration Levels

Traditional classifications include:

  • SSI → Small-Scale Integration.
  • MSI → Medium-Scale Integration.
  • LSI → Large-Scale Integration.
  • VLSI → Very-Large-Scale Integration.
  • ULSI is sometimes used for extremely high integration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

VLSI → Very-Large-Scale Integration

92. VLSI
  • VLSI technology integrates very large numbers of transistors on a single chip.
  • Modern processors and memory chips use VLSI technologies.
  • VLSI enabled compact computers and mobile devices.
93. Microprocessor
  • A microprocessor is a programmable digital processor implemented mainly on one integrated circuit.
  • It contains the central processing unit.
  • It performs arithmetic, logic and control operations.
  • It requires external memory and peripheral interfaces in many systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Microprocessor → CPU on a Chip

94. CPU

CPU stands for Central Processing Unit.

Major functional parts include:

  • Arithmetic Logic Unit.
  • Control Unit.
  • Registers.
  • CPU executes program instructions.
95. Arithmetic Logic Unit
  • ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit.
  • It performs arithmetic operations.
  • It performs logical operations.
  • Addition, subtraction and comparisons are examples.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ALU → Arithmetic + Logic

96. Control Unit
  • Control unit coordinates processor operations.
  • It fetches and decodes instructions.
  • It directs data movement between different parts of the computer.
  • It controls execution sequence.
97. Microcontroller
  • A microcontroller combines CPU, memory and input/output peripherals on one chip or package.
  • It is designed mainly for embedded-control applications.
  • Washing machines, automobiles, toys and appliances use microcontrollers.
  • It can operate without a full general-purpose computer system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Microcontroller → CPU + Memory + I/O on One Chip

98. Microprocessor vs Microcontroller
  • Microprocessor focuses primarily on CPU functions.
  • Microcontroller integrates CPU, memory and peripherals.
  • Microprocessors are common in general-purpose computing.
  • Microcontrollers are common in embedded systems.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Microprocessor ≠ Microcontroller.

99. Embedded System
  • An embedded system is a computer-based control system built into a larger device.
  • It performs a dedicated function.
  • Examples include washing machines, digital cameras and vehicle-control modules.
  • Microcontrollers are widely used in embedded systems.
100. Sensor
  • A sensor detects a physical, chemical or biological quantity.
  • It converts the quantity into a usable signal.
  • Temperature sensors detect temperature.
  • Photodiodes detect light.
  • Pressure sensors detect pressure.
  • Motion sensors detect movement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sensor → Physical Quantity to Signal

101. Transducer
  • A transducer converts energy from one form to another.
  • A microphone converts sound into electrical signals.
  • A loudspeaker converts electrical signals into sound.
  • Sensors are often transducers.
102. Microphone
  • A microphone converts sound energy into an electrical signal.
  • Dynamic microphones use electromagnetic induction.
  • Condenser microphones use changing capacitance.
  • Microphones provide input signals to electronic systems.
103. Loudspeaker
  • A loudspeaker converts electrical signals into mechanical vibration and sound.
  • Current through a voice coil interacts with a magnetic field.
  • The diaphragm vibrates and produces sound waves.
104. ADC
  • ADC stands for Analog-to-Digital Converter.
  • It converts a continuous analog signal into digital numerical data.
  • ADCs are used in digital audio, sensors and data acquisition.
  • Resolution is commonly expressed in bits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ADC → Analog to Digital

105. DAC
  • DAC stands for Digital-to-Analog Converter.
  • It converts digital data into an analog electrical signal.
  • DACs are used in audio output and control systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

DAC → Digital to Analog

106. Sampling
  • Sampling measures an analog signal at discrete time intervals.
  • Sampling is required before digital representation.
  • Higher sampling frequency captures faster signal changes.
  • Sampling theory is important in digital audio and communication.
107. Operational Amplifier
  • Operational amplifier is abbreviated as op-amp.
  • It is a high-gain differential voltage amplifier.
  • It has inverting and non-inverting inputs.
  • Op-amps are used in amplifiers, filters, comparators and mathematical circuits.
  • Ideal op-amp has extremely high input impedance and very low output impedance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Op-Amp → High-Gain Differential Amplifier

108. Comparator
  • A comparator compares two input voltages.
  • Output changes according to which input is greater.
  • Comparators are used in threshold detectors and control systems.
  • Op-amps can be used as comparators in basic applications.
109. Amplifier
  • An amplifier increases signal voltage, current or power using energy from a power supply.
  • Voltage amplifier increases voltage amplitude.
  • Power amplifier delivers greater power to a load.
  • Transistors and op-amps are common amplifier devices.
110. Gain
  • Gain is the ratio of output signal to input signal.
  • Voltage gain = Vout/Vin.
  • Current gain = Iout/Iin.
  • Power gain = Pout/Pin.
  • Gain may be expressed as a simple ratio or in decibels.
111. Feedback
  • Feedback returns part of the output signal to the input.
  • Negative feedback can improve stability and reduce distortion.
  • Positive feedback can support oscillation.
  • Oscillator circuits use controlled positive feedback.
112. Capacitor in Electronics
  • A capacitor stores electric charge.
  • It can block steady DC after charging while allowing changing signals to pass depending on frequency.
  • Capacitors are used for filtering, coupling, timing and energy storage.
  • Capacitance is measured in farads.
113. Resistor in Electronics
  • A resistor limits current.
  • It creates voltage drops.
  • Resistors are used for biasing, current limiting and voltage division.
  • Resistance is measured in ohms.
114. Inductor
  • An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field.
  • It opposes rapid changes in current.
  • Inductance is measured in henry.
  • Inductors are used in filters, power supplies and tuned circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Inductance Unit → Henry

115. Transformer in Electronics
  • A transformer transfers AC energy through electromagnetic induction.
  • It can step voltage up or down.
  • It provides electrical isolation in many circuits.
  • Transformers require changing magnetic flux.
116. PCB
  • PCB stands for Printed Circuit Board.
  • It mechanically supports electronic components.
  • Copper tracks provide electrical connections.
  • PCBs replace much point-to-point wiring.
  • Modern devices may use multilayer PCBs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PCB → Printed Circuit Board

117. Soldering
  • Soldering joins electronic components using a low-melting metal alloy.
  • Solder creates electrical and mechanical connections.
  • Excessive heating can damage semiconductor components.
  • Lead-free solders are increasingly used.
118. CRO
  • CRO stands for Cathode-Ray Oscilloscope.
  • It displays electrical signals as waveforms.
  • Horizontal axis commonly represents time.
  • Vertical axis commonly represents voltage.
  • It can measure amplitude, period and frequency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CRO → Displays Electrical Waveforms

119. Cathode-Ray Tube
  • CRT stands for Cathode-Ray Tube.
  • It uses an electron beam in a vacuum tube.
  • Electron beam strikes a fluorescent screen.
  • CRTs were historically used in televisions, monitors and oscilloscopes.
  • Modern flat-panel displays have largely replaced CRTs.
120. Multimeter
  • A multimeter measures electrical quantities.
  • It commonly measures voltage, current and resistance.
  • Digital multimeters are widely used in electronics.
  • Some multimeters also measure capacitance, frequency and diode behaviour.
121. Electronic Display Types

Common display technologies include:

  • LED.
  • LCD.
  • OLED.
  • They differ in how light is produced or controlled.
122. LCD
  • LCD stands for Liquid Crystal Display.
  • Liquid crystals control transmission of light.
  • LCDs generally require a backlight unless designed for reflective operation.
  • They are used in monitors, televisions, calculators and instruments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LCD → Liquid Crystal Display

123. OLED
  • OLED stands for Organic Light-Emitting Diode.
  • Organic semiconductor layers emit light directly when electrically driven.
  • Individual pixels can emit their own light.
  • OLED displays do not require a conventional backlight.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

OLED → Self-Emissive Organic LED Pixels

124. LED Display
  • LED displays use light-emitting diodes.
  • Large outdoor displays may use individual LEDs directly.
  • Many so-called LED televisions are LCD panels using LED backlighting.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Most “LED TVs” are LCD displays with LED backlights, not direct-view LED pixels.

125. Memory — Basic Electronics Link
  • Electronic memory stores digital information.
  • RAM allows temporary read/write storage.
  • ROM stores data that is non-volatile in basic descriptions.
  • Flash memory is non-volatile semiconductor memory.
  • Memory cells are built from transistor-based circuits.
126. RAM
  • RAM stands for Random Access Memory.
  • It is used for temporary working data.
  • Most conventional RAM loses stored data when power is removed.
  • RAM is therefore usually volatile memory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

RAM → Volatile

127. ROM
  • ROM stands for Read-Only Memory.
  • It is non-volatile.
  • Basic firmware can be stored in ROM-type memory.
  • Modern ROM technologies include programmable forms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ROM → Non-Volatile

128. Flash Memory
  • Flash memory is non-volatile semiconductor memory.
  • It retains data without electrical power.
  • USB drives and solid-state storage use flash memory.
  • NAND flash is widely used for data storage.
129. Solid-State Device
  • A solid-state device operates mainly using charge carriers in solid materials.
  • Semiconductor diodes and transistors are solid-state devices.
  • Solid-state devices contain no vacuum-tube electron beam.
  • They are generally compact and reliable.
130. Vacuum Tube
  • Vacuum tubes control electron flow through vacuum.
  • They preceded transistors in electronic equipment.
  • They are larger and consume more power than semiconductor devices.
  • Vacuum tubes are still used in specialised high-power and audio applications.
131. Transistor Revolution
  • Transistors enabled miniaturisation of electronics.
  • They reduced power consumption.
  • They increased reliability.
  • Integrated circuits allowed millions and later billions of transistors to be placed on chips.
  • This development enabled modern computing.
132. Moore's Law
  • Moore's Law was an observation by Gordon Moore regarding rapid growth in transistor counts on integrated circuits over time.
  • It was historically expressed as approximate doubling on a roughly regular timescale.
  • It is an industry observation, not a physical law.
  • Its exact cadence has changed as semiconductor technology has evolved.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Moore's Law → Technological trend, not fundamental law of physics.

133. Semiconductor Fabrication
  • Integrated circuits are fabricated on semiconductor wafers.
  • Silicon wafers are widely used.
  • Photolithography creates microscopic circuit patterns.
  • Doping forms semiconductor regions.
  • Multiple layers create transistors and interconnections.
134. Photolithography
  • Photolithography uses patterned light exposure to define microscopic features.
  • It is fundamental to chip manufacturing.
  • Shorter wavelengths allow smaller features under suitable optical systems.
  • Advanced fabrication uses sophisticated ultraviolet lithography.
135. Clean Room
  • Semiconductor fabrication occurs in extremely clean environments.
  • Tiny dust particles can damage microscopic circuit patterns.
  • Air filtration and contamination control are essential.
136. E-Waste
  • Electronic waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment.
  • It may contain valuable metals and hazardous materials.
  • Proper collection and recycling reduce environmental contamination.
  • Informal burning or acid treatment can release toxic substances.
137. Electronic Sensors in Everyday Life
  • Thermistor → Temperature.
  • LDR → Light.
  • Photodiode → Light.
  • Microphone → Sound.
  • Accelerometer → Acceleration.
  • Pressure sensor → Pressure.
  • Hall sensor → Magnetic field.
  • Proximity sensor → Nearby objects.
138. Hall Effect
  • Hall effect produces a voltage across a conductor or semiconductor carrying current in a magnetic field.
  • Hall voltage is perpendicular to current and magnetic field.
  • Hall sensors detect magnetic fields.
  • Edwin Hall discovered the effect in 1879.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hall Effect → Magnetic Field Sensor → Edwin Hall

139. Infrared Sensor
  • Infrared sensors detect or emit infrared radiation.
  • They are used in remote controls, motion detectors and thermal sensing.
  • PIR stands for Passive Infrared sensor.
  • PIR sensors detect changes in infrared radiation from warm objects.
140. Electronic Remote Control
  • Many television remote controls use infrared LEDs.
  • Digital codes modulate the infrared light.
  • A photodetector in the television receives the signal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TV Remote → Infrared

141. Optocoupler
  • An optocoupler transfers a signal using light between electrically isolated circuits.
  • It commonly contains an LED and photodetector.
  • It provides electrical isolation.
142. Relay vs Transistor Switch
  • Electromechanical relay uses physical contacts controlled by an electromagnet.
  • Transistor switching has no mechanical contact.
  • Transistors switch much faster.
  • Relays can provide strong electrical isolation and switch different load types.
143. Power Electronics
  • Power electronics controls and converts electrical power using semiconductor switches.
  • Devices include diodes, MOSFETs, IGBTs and thyristors.
  • Applications include motor drives, solar inverters, chargers and electric vehicles.
144. Inverter
  • An electronic inverter converts DC into AC.
  • Solar-power systems use inverters to convert panel DC into AC.
  • UPS systems also use inverter circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Inverter → DC to AC

145. Rectifier vs Inverter
  • Rectifier → AC to DC.
  • Inverter → DC to AC.
📌 Must-Memorise

AC → DC = Rectifier

DC → AC = Inverter

146. UPS
  • UPS stands for Uninterruptible Power Supply.
  • It provides temporary electrical power when mains supply fails.
  • It usually contains battery storage and inverter electronics.
  • UPS systems protect computers and other sensitive equipment.
147. SMPS
  • SMPS stands for Switched-Mode Power Supply.
  • It converts electrical power efficiently using high-frequency switching.
  • It is smaller and more efficient than many traditional linear supplies.
  • Computers and chargers commonly use SMPS circuits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

SMPS → Switched-Mode Power Supply

148. Voltage Regulator
  • A voltage regulator maintains output voltage within a desired range.
  • Zener diodes can provide simple voltage regulation.
  • Integrated regulator ICs provide better regulation.
  • Modern power supplies often use switching regulators.
149. Electronic Fuse / Protection
  • Electronic circuits use fuses, circuit breakers and semiconductor protection.
  • Diodes can protect against reverse polarity.
  • Surge suppressors protect against transient overvoltage.
  • Proper grounding protects equipment and users.
150. Important Electronics Formulae
  • Diode junction basics → Forward bias allows strong current.
  • Transistor current → IE = IC + IB.
  • BJT current gain → β = IC/IB.
  • Voltage gain → Av = Vout/Vin.
  • Frequency → f = 1/T.
  • Capacitor relation → Q = CV.
  • Capacitor energy → ½CV².
  • Electrical power → P = VI.
  • Resistance → V = IR.
151. Important Units
  • Resistance → Ohm.
  • Capacitance → Farad.
  • Inductance → Henry.
  • Current → Ampere.
  • Voltage → Volt.
  • Frequency → Hertz.
  • Semiconductor band-gap energy → Electronvolt.
  • Gain → Usually dimensionless or expressed in decibels.
152. Important Scientist–Fact Pairs
  • George Boole → Boolean algebra.
  • John Bardeen → Transistor.
  • Walter Brattain → Transistor.
  • William Shockley → Transistor.
  • Jack Kilby → Integrated circuit.
  • Robert Noyce → Integrated circuit.
  • Gordon Moore → Moore's Law.
  • Edwin Hall → Hall effect.
  • Albert Einstein → Stimulated emission, relevant to laser electronics.
153. Important Dates
  • Hall effect discovered → 1879.
  • First transistor demonstrated → 1947.
  • Transistor Nobel Prize → 1956.
  • Early working integrated circuit by Jack Kilby → 1958.
  • Noyce's monolithic IC development → 1959.
  • Kilby Nobel recognition → 2000.
154. Must-Memorise Semiconductor Pairs
  • Intrinsic → Pure.
  • Extrinsic → Doped.
  • n-type → Electrons majority.
  • p-type → Holes majority.
  • Pentavalent → Donor.
  • Trivalent → Acceptor.
  • Phosphorus → n-type dopant.
  • Boron → p-type dopant.
  • Silicon → Most common semiconductor.
  • Germanium → Early semiconductor material.
155. Must-Memorise Device Pairs
  • Diode → One-way conduction.
  • Rectifier → AC to DC.
  • Zener → Voltage regulation.
  • LED → Emits light.
  • Photodiode → Detects light.
  • Solar cell → Light to electricity.
  • LDR → Light-dependent resistance.
  • Transistor → Amplifier/switch.
  • FET → Voltage-controlled device.
  • SCR → Power switching.
  • IC → Many devices on one chip.
  • ADC → Analog to digital.
  • DAC → Digital to analog.
  • Inverter → DC to AC.
156. Must-Memorise Logic Gates
  • AND → All inputs 1 gives 1.
  • OR → Any input 1 gives 1.
  • NOT → Reverses input.
  • NAND → Universal.
  • NOR → Universal.
  • XOR → Different inputs give 1.
  • XNOR → Same inputs give 1.
157. TNPSC Traps
  • Semiconductor conductivity lies between conductor and insulator.
  • Silicon has four valence electrons.
  • Semiconductor resistance generally decreases with increasing temperature.
  • Intrinsic semiconductor is pure.
  • Extrinsic semiconductor is doped.
  • n-type majority carriers are electrons.
  • p-type majority carriers are holes.
  • n-type is electrically neutral overall.
  • p-type is electrically neutral overall.
  • Pentavalent impurity produces n-type material.
  • Trivalent impurity produces p-type material.
  • Hole is not a proton.
  • A diode contains a p–n junction.
  • Forward bias reduces depletion width.
  • Reverse bias increases depletion width.
  • Rectifier converts AC to DC.
  • Inverter converts DC to AC.
  • Bridge rectifier commonly uses four diodes.
  • Zener diode operates in reverse breakdown for voltage regulation.
  • LED is forward biased.
  • Photodiode is commonly reverse biased.
  • Solar cell uses photovoltaic effect.
  • LDR resistance falls as illumination rises.
  • Transistor is used as switch and amplifier.
  • BJT has emitter, base and collector.
  • IE = IC + IB.
  • FET is voltage controlled.
  • NAND and NOR are universal gates.
  • XOR gives 1 for unequal inputs.
  • Flip-flop stores one bit.
  • 1 byte = 8 bits.
  • Microprocessor and microcontroller are not identical.
  • IC contains many electronic components on one chip.
  • Most modern digital ICs rely heavily on MOSFETs.
  • RAM is usually volatile.
  • ROM and flash are non-volatile.
  • LCD and OLED are different technologies.
  • Most commercial “LED TVs” are LCDs with LED backlights.
158. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Semiconductor → Si, Ge.
  • Si → 4 valence electrons.
  • Intrinsic → Pure.
  • Extrinsic → Doped.
  • n-type → Electron.
  • p-type → Hole.
  • Donor → Pentavalent.
  • Acceptor → Trivalent.
  • Diode → One way.
  • Forward bias → Conducts.
  • Reverse bias → Blocks mostly.
  • Si diode → ~0.7 V.
  • Ge diode → ~0.3 V.
  • Rectifier → AC to DC.
  • Inverter → DC to AC.
  • Zener → Regulator.
  • LED → Light output.
  • Photodiode → Light input.
  • Solar cell → Photovoltaic.
  • LDR → Light ↑, R ↓.
  • Transistor → Switch/amplifier.
  • BJT → E, B, C.
  • IE → IC + IB.
  • FET → Voltage controlled.
  • NAND/NOR → Universal.
  • Flip-flop → 1 bit.
  • Byte → 8 bits.
  • IC → Chip.
  • Microprocessor → CPU.
  • Microcontroller → CPU + Memory + I/O.
  • ADC → Analog to digital.
  • DAC → Digital to analog.

  • Another elemental semiconductor? → Germanium.
  • Atomic number of silicon? → 14.

  • Pure semiconductor called? → Intrinsic semiconductor.

  • Process of adding impurity? → Doping.
  • Two extrinsic semiconductor types? → n-type and p-type.

  • Minority carrier in n-type? → Holes.
  • Majority carrier in p-type? → Holes.
  • Minority carrier in p-type? → Electrons.

  • Reverse bias effect? → Widens it.

  • Device used for voltage regulation? → Zener diode.
  • Zener diode operates mainly in? → Reverse breakdown region.
  • LED stands for? → Light-Emitting Diode.
  • LED usually operates in? → Forward bias.
  • Why does LED emit light? → Electron-hole recombination releases photons.
  • Photodiode function? → Detect light.
  • Photodiode normally operated in? → Reverse bias.
  • Solar cell works on? → Photovoltaic effect.
  • Solar cell converts? → Light directly into electrical energy.
  • Solar cell output? → DC.
  • LDR stands for? → Light Dependent Resistor.
  • LDR resistance when light increases? → Decreases.
  • Thermistor senses? → Temperature.

  • Three BJT terminals? → Emitter, base and collector.

  • Common-emitter current gain? → β = IC/IB.
  • FET stands for? → Field-Effect Transistor.
  • FET is mainly current- or voltage-controlled? → Voltage-controlled.
  • MOSFET stands for? → Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor.

  • SCR stands for? → Silicon Controlled Rectifier.
  • SCR mainly used for? → Power switching/control.

  • Digital signal means? → Discrete levels.
  • Binary digits? → 0 and 1.
  • One binary digit called? → Bit.
  • One nibble? → 4 bits.
  • One byte? → 8 bits.

  • OR output is 1 when? → At least one input is 1.

  • XOR output is 1 when? → Inputs are different.
  • XNOR output is 1 when? → Inputs are the same.
  • Boolean algebra developed by? → George Boole.
  • Circuit with no memory? → Combinational circuit.
  • Circuit with memory? → Sequential circuit.
  • Basic one-bit memory element? → Flip-flop.
  • A flip-flop stores? → 1 bit.
  • Registers are built from? → Flip-flops.
  • Counter does? → Advances through a sequence of digital states.
  • Stable timing device based on piezoelectric effect? → Quartz crystal oscillator.
  • IC stands for? → Integrated Circuit.
  • What is an IC? → Many electronic components fabricated on one semiconductor chip.
  • Scientists associated with integrated circuit? → Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce.
  • Kilby's early IC demonstrated in? → 1958.
